title: Descriptive Statistics
description: Mean, median, quartiles, the interquartile range, standard deviation and comparing distributions

notes.heading: Measures of Central Tendency
notes.body:
Three numbers summarise the centre of a data set:

• **Mean** — the arithmetic average, $\bar{x} = \dfrac{\sum x}{n}$, where $n$ is the number of values.
• **Median** — the middle value once the data are in order (the average of the two middle values if $n$ is even).
• **Mode** — the most frequent value; a set can have several modes or none.

💡 **Worked Example** — For $3, 7, 9, 11, 15$: the mean is $\dfrac{45}{5} = 9$ and the median is also 9.

🔑 The mean uses every value, so a single **outlier** drags it; the median depends only on position and is barely affected. That difference decides which measure to quote when a distribution is skewed.

notes.heading: Quartiles, the IQR and Box Plots
notes.body:
Order the data and split it into four parts:

• $Q_1$ is the **lower quartile** — the median of the lower half.
• $Q_2$ is the **median**.
• $Q_3$ is the **upper quartile** — the median of the upper half.

The **interquartile range** is $\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$: the spread of the middle 50% of the data.

A **box plot** shows the five-number summary — minimum, $Q_1$, median, $Q_3$, maximum — with the box from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$ and a line at the median. Whiskers run to the smallest and largest values that are not outliers.

💡 **Worked Example** — For $4, 6, 9, 11, 15, 18, 21, 25$: the lower half is $4, 6, 9, 11$, so $Q_1 = \dfrac{6+9}{2} = 7.5$; the upper half is $15, 18, 21, 25$, so $Q_3 = \dfrac{18+21}{2} = 19.5$. Hence $\text{IQR} = 12$.

📌 The IQR is a **robust** measure: it ignores extreme values entirely, which is why box plots are used to compare skewed data sets.

illustration.alt: A box plot with the minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile and maximum labelled, the interquartile range bracketed, and an outlier marked beyond the upper boundary.
illustration.caption: The box spans the middle half of the data, and anything past Q₃ + 1.5 IQR is flagged rather than included in the whisker.

notes.heading: Outliers
notes.body:
A value is treated as an **outlier** if it lies more than $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ beyond the nearer quartile:
$$\text{lower boundary} = Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR} \qquad \text{upper boundary} = Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR}$$

💡 **Worked Example** — A set has $Q_1 = 10$ and $Q_3 = 20$, so $\text{IQR} = 10$ and $1.5\,\text{IQR} = 15$. The boundaries are
$$10 - 15 = -5 \qquad\text{and}\qquad 20 + 15 = 35$$
A value of 40 lies above 35, so it is an outlier; a value of 32 does not, so it is not.

⚠️ **Common mistake** — Judging an outlier by comparing it with the maximum or by eye. Compute the two boundaries, then compare.

📌 Being an outlier is not by itself a reason to delete a value. It is a flag that prompts you to check the data — a measurement error is removed, a genuine extreme value is kept and reported.

notes.heading: Standard Deviation and Variance
notes.body:
The **standard deviation** measures the typical distance of a value from the mean. For a list of $n$ values,
$$\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n}}$$
and the **variance** is $\sigma^2$. Your calculator offers two keys: $\sigma_n$ (the population standard deviation) and $s_{n-1}$ (the sample standard deviation). DP questions specify which is wanted; if they do not, use $\sigma_n$.

💡 **Worked Example** — For $2, 4, 4, 4, 6$ the mean is 4, and the squared deviations are $4, 0, 0, 0, 4$:
$$\sigma^2 = \dfrac{8}{5} = 1.6 \;\Longrightarrow\; \sigma = \sqrt{1.6} \approx 1.26$$

⚠️ **Common mistake** — Squaring the mean instead of each deviation, or dividing by the wrong $n$. Better still: enter the list into the GDC and read $\sigma_n$ directly, then check it is plausible against the spread of the data.

📌 The standard deviation has the same units as the data, so it can be compared directly with the mean; the variance cannot.

notes.heading: Grouped Data and Mid-interval Values
notes.body:
When data arrive in classes, the individual values are lost, so every value in a class is represented by its **mid-interval value** (the average of the class boundaries).

Then $\bar{x} = \dfrac{\sum f x_m}{\sum f}$, where $f$ is the frequency and $x_m$ the mid-interval value.

💡 **Worked Example** —

| Class | Frequency | Mid-interval $x_m$ |
|---|---|---|
| $0 \le x < 10$ | 3 | 5 |
| $10 \le x < 20$ | 7 | 15 |
| $20 \le x < 30$ | 10 | 25 |

$$\bar{x} = \dfrac{3(5) + 7(15) + 10(25)}{20} = \dfrac{15 + 105 + 250}{20} = \dfrac{370}{20} = 18.5$$

⚠️ **Common mistake** — Using the class boundary rather than the midpoint, or using $0 \le x < 10$ to mean $x = 10$.

📌 The estimate is only as good as the mid-interval assumption: it is exact when values are spread evenly inside each class, and approximate otherwise.

notes.heading: Comparing Distributions
notes.body:
When asked to compare two distributions, comment on a **measure of centre** and a **measure of spread**, in the context of the question.

• Symmetric data: compare the **mean and standard deviation**.
• Skewed data or data with outliers: compare the **median and interquartile range**, because both are robust.

💡 **Worked Example** — Set $P$ has median 8 and IQR 5; set $Q$ has median 9 and IQR 12. Then $Q$ typically has the higher values (larger median), but $P$ is much more consistent (smaller IQR).

🔑 A full comparison sentence contains: which is larger, by how much, and what it means. "The median mark is 1 higher in $Q$, so a typical student in $Q$ scored slightly higher, but $P$'s marks are more consistent."

⚠️ **Common mistake** — Comparing only the centres, or quoting two numbers with no interpretation. Marks are awarded for the comparison, not the numbers.

notes.heading: Cumulative Frequency and Percentiles
notes.body:
A **cumulative frequency** table records a running total, so the entry in a row tells you how many values are **less than** the upper boundary of that class.

Plot cumulative frequency against the class upper boundary. Then:
• the median is at cumulative frequency $\dfrac{n}{2}$;
• the lower quartile is at $\dfrac{n}{4}$;
• the upper quartile is at $\dfrac{3n}{4}$;
• the $p$th percentile is at $\dfrac{pn}{100}$.

💡 **Worked Example** — With $n = 40$, the median is read at cumulative frequency 20, $Q_1$ at 10 and $Q_3$ at 30.

**Exam technique**
• Sort the data before finding the median or quartiles — the mean is the only measure that does not need ordered data.
• State the units with every measure of centre or spread.
• For a box-plot question, identify which feature (median, IQR, outlier) the question is really testing before doing arithmetic.

questions.explanation: With five values in order, the median is the third: 9.
The range is the largest value minus the smallest: $12 - 2 = 10$.
The value 3 occurs twice and every other value once, so the mode is 3.

questions.stem: Which measure of central tendency is most affected by a single extreme value?
questions.explanation: The mean adds every value, so one extreme value changes it substantially; the median and mode depend only on position or frequency.

questions.stem: The mean of five numbers is 12. Four of the numbers are $8, 10, 14, 16$. Find the fifth number.
questions.explanation: The total is $5 \times 12 = 60$, and the four known values total 48, so the fifth is $60 - 48 = 12$.

questions.stem: For the data $4, 6, 9, 11, 15, 18, 21, 25$, find the interquartile range.
questions.explanation: The lower half is $4, 6, 9, 11$ so $Q_1 = 7.5$; the upper half is $15, 18, 21, 25$ so $Q_3 = 19.5$. Hence $\text{IQR} = 19.5 - 7.5 = 12$.

questions.stem: A data set has lower quartile 10 and upper quartile 20. Find the upper boundary above which a value would be an outlier.
Find the variance of the data $2, 4, 4, 4, 6$.
questions.explanation: The mean is 4, so the squared deviations are 4, 0, 0, 0, 4. Their total is 8 and $n = 5$, giving variance $\dfrac{8}{5} = 1.6$. (The standard deviation is $\sqrt{1.6} \approx 1.26$.)

questions.stem: A constant 5 is added to every value in a data set. Which statement is correct?
choices: the mean increases by 5 and the standard deviation is unchanged
the standard deviation increases by 5 and the mean is unchanged
both the mean and the standard deviation increase by 5
the mean is unchanged and the standard deviation increases by 5
questions.explanation: Shifting every value by 5 shifts the mean by 5 but leaves the spread, and therefore the standard deviation and IQR, exactly as they were.

questions.stem: A data set has standard deviation 4. Every value is multiplied by 3. What is the new standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Multiplying every value by 3 multiplies every deviation by 3, so the standard deviation becomes $3 \times 4 = 12$. (The variance would be multiplied by 9.)

questions.stem: Estimate the mean of the grouped data: 3 values in $0 \le x < 10$, 7 values in $10 \le x < 20$ and 10 values in $20 \le x < 30$.
A data set of 20 values has mean 30. A further value of 100 is added to the data. Which statement best describes the effect?
choices: both the mean and the median increase by the same amount
the median increases by more than the mean
the mean increases and the median changes little
questions.explanation: The new mean is $\dfrac{20(30) + 100}{21} = \dfrac{700}{21} \approx 33.3$, so it rises by about 3.3. The median is a positional measure, so adding one large value moves it very little.

questions.stem: Set $A$ is $2, 3, 4, 5, 6$ and set $B$ is $4, 4, 4, 4, 4$. Which set has the greater standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Set $B$ has every value equal to the mean, so its standard deviation is 0. Set $A$'s values are spread around its mean of 4, so its standard deviation is greater.

questions.stem: Set $P$ has $Q_1 = 5$ and $Q_3 = 10$; set $Q$ has $Q_1 = 4$ and $Q_3 = 16$. Which set has the greater interquartile range?
questions.explanation: $P$ has $\text{IQR} = 5$ and $Q$ has $\text{IQR} = 12$, so set $Q$ has the greater interquartile range.

questions.stem: A data set has mean 20 and standard deviation 4. Every value is multiplied by 2 and then 3 is added. Find the new mean and the new standard deviation.
questions.explanation: Multiplication acts on both centre and spread: the mean becomes $2(20) = 40$ and the standard deviation $2(4) = 8$. Adding 3 then shifts the centre only, giving mean 43 and standard deviation 8.
